title: Immigrant Stories
description: Ten family memories and short history texts about people who came to America: Ellis Island, an Irish cook in Boston, the Chinese railroad workers, a baker from Naples, a German clockmaker, a mail carrier from Mexico, a nurse from Vietnam, a museum visit, a citizenship ceremony and the Lunar New Year in Chinatown.

lessons.title: Ellis Island
lessons.summary: A short history of the island in New York Harbor where millions of immigrants entered America.
lessons.text:
For more than 60 years, Ellis Island was the front door to America. This small island in New York Harbor opened as an immigration station on January 1, 1892, and it closed in 1954. During those years, about 12 million immigrants passed through it. Today, millions of Americans have at least one family member who arrived there.

For many years, the station was run by the Bureau of Immigration, a part of the federal government. The bureau's job was to decide who could enter the country. On the ships' passenger lists, every person who was not a citizen was called an "alien." The word sounds strange today, but then it simply meant a person from another country.

Most immigrants came from Europe: from Ireland, Italy, Germany, Poland, Greece and many other countries. Arab families from Syria and Lebanon, for example, also passed through the island, and many Arab immigrants settled in a small neighborhood in lower Manhattan.

Passengers who had traveled in first or second class were usually checked on the ship. Everyone else took a small boat to the island. There, they carried their bags up a long flight of stairs to a huge room called the Great Hall. Doctors in uniform stood at the top of the stairs and watched them climb. They were looking for signs of illness. If a doctor thought that a person might have an illness, he marked a letter on the person's coat, and that person had to see another doctor.

The Great Hall was divided into long lines by metal rails. At the end of each line, an officer in uniform asked about 30 questions: What is your name? Where are you going? Do you have a job? Many immigrants did not speak English, so they were often confused. Helpers who spoke dozens of languages could translate the questions and the answers. When they translated, a confused traveler usually felt much calmer.

Even though the day was long and tiring, most people were finished in a few hours. Only about 2 percent were not allowed to stay. After the questions, the stairs down from the Great Hall were divided into three parts, and each part led to a different exit. One exit was for the boat to New York City, one was for the trains to other states, and one was for people who had to wait longer. At the exit to the boat, families often met again after months or even years apart.

Questions:
When did Ellis Island open and close?
It opened on January 1, 1892, and it closed in 1954.
What was the job of the Bureau of Immigration?
Its job was to decide who could enter the country.
What did the word "alien" mean at that time?
It simply meant a person from another country.
Why did the doctors watch people climb the stairs?
They were looking for signs of illness.
How did the helpers make the questions easier?
They translated the questions and the answers, so the confused travelers felt calmer.
Where did families often meet again?
They often met again at the exit to the boat.

lessons.title: Bridget's Book of Poems
lessons.summary: A woman tells what she knows about her great-great-grandmother, who came from Ireland to Boston in 1891.
lessons.text:
My great-great-grandmother, Bridget Walsh, came to America from Ireland in 1891. She was 19 years old, and she traveled alone. I never met her, of course, but my family has told so many stories about her that I feel I know her.

Bridget grew up on a small farm in the west of Ireland. The landscape there is green and rocky, with low stone walls, small white houses and the wide Atlantic Ocean. When she left, her only possessions were a small bag of clothes, a little money and a book of Irish poems. That book is now my most important possession. It sits on a shelf in my living room.

In Boston, Bridget worked as a cook for a rich family. A few years later, she married Michael Burke, who had also come from Ireland. Michael worked for the city. His job was to dig long, deep holes in the streets for the new water pipes. He dug in summer and in winter. Thanks to men like him, the people of Boston had clean water in their pipes.

Bridget had a reputation in the neighborhood for two things. First, she had a cure for almost every illness. For a cold, her cure was hot tea with honey and lemon. Not all of her cures really worked, of course, but people naturally felt better when someone took care of them.

Second, she had a reputation as a wonderful storyteller. Bridget had a lot of charm. When she was in a good mood, she sat by the fire and read poems aloud to her children. Even when she was in a bad mood, a poem could change her mood. Her daughter said years later that Bridget's charm made everyone in the room smile.

Naturally, Bridget wanted her children to love Ireland too. They never saw it, but she described the landscape so well that they could almost see it: the green hills, the stone walls and the gray sea.

Last year, I finally visited Ireland. When I saw the landscape with my own eyes, I understood why Bridget had loved it so much. I took her book with me, and I read one of her favorite poems aloud by the sea. If she had been there, I think she would have smiled.

Questions:
When did Bridget come to America?
She came to America in 1891, when she was 19 years old.
What were her only possessions when she left Ireland?
Her only possessions were a small bag of clothes, a little money and a book of Irish poems.
What was Michael's job?
His job was to dig long, deep holes in the streets for the new water pipes.
What was Bridget's cure for a cold?
Her cure for a cold was hot tea with honey and lemon.
What did Bridget do when she was in a good mood?
She sat by the fire and read poems aloud to her children.
What did the writer do in Ireland?
She read one of Bridget's favorite poems aloud by the sea.

lessons.title: The Railroad Through the Mountains
lessons.summary: A short history of the Chinese workers who built the western part of the first railroad across America.
lessons.text:
In 1863, the United States began one of the biggest building projects in its history: a railroad across the country. Before it was built, a trip from New York to California could take months. Two companies shared the work. The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, California, and built toward the east. Meanwhile, the Union Pacific started in Nebraska and built toward the west. Its workers were primarily Irish immigrants and men who had fought in the Civil War.

The Central Pacific had a big problem: it could not find enough workers. In 1865, it hired a small group of Chinese workers, and the results were impressive. The Chinese workers were fast, careful and consistent. Because their work was so consistent from day to day, the company soon hired thousands more. By 1868, the Central Pacific's workers were primarily Chinese.

The hardest part was the Sierra Nevada, a wall of high mountains that the railroad had to go through. The workers used powder to blast tunnels through hard rock. After each blast, they carried away the broken rock and got ready for the next blast. On some days, they moved forward less than a foot. The winters were long and cold, but the workers kept going regardless of the weather. They worked regardless of the deep snow, too. Meanwhile, far to the east, the Union Pacific workers were crossing the flat plains much faster.

In some places, the workers built the track along the side of a mountain. In one famous place called Cape Horn, the track follows a long curve high above a river. The rails bend slowly around the mountain, and the view of the valley from the train is impressive. Engineers planned every curve and every bend, so that the trains could climb safely.

On May 10, 1869, the two railroads met at Promontory Summit, in Utah, and a golden spike was put into the last piece of track. Now a trip across the country took about a week instead of months. The railroad became one of the most important pieces of infrastructure in the country. It connected the East and the West, and other infrastructure, such as roads and towns, grew along it.

For many years, the Chinese workers did not get the recognition they deserved. In the famous photograph from Promontory Summit, almost none of them can be seen. Recognition came slowly. In 2014, the Department of Labor finally added them to its Hall of Honor.

Questions:
Where did the two companies start?
The Central Pacific started in Sacramento, and the Union Pacific started in Nebraska.
Why did the Central Pacific hire thousands more Chinese workers?
It hired more of them because their work was fast, careful and consistent.
How did the workers make tunnels through the mountains?
They used powder to blast tunnels through hard rock.
What happens at Cape Horn?
The track follows a long curve high above a river, and the rails bend slowly around the mountain.
When did the Chinese workers finally get some recognition?
In 2014, the Department of Labor added them to its Hall of Honor.

lessons.title: Salvatore's Pizza
lessons.summary: A man remembers his great-grandfather, a baker from Naples, and tries to make his pizza.
lessons.text:
My great-grandfather, Salvatore Russo, was born in Naples, Italy, in 1890. Naples is a beautiful old city by the sea. It has a royal palace, where kings once lived, and one of the oldest opera houses in Europe, the San Carlo theater. As a boy, Salvatore often walked past the palace and stood outside the theater in the evening to listen to the music. He was too poor to go inside.

Salvatore came to New York in 1909. He was 19, and he had a very practical plan: find a job, save money and open his own bakery. His first job was in a bakery in Manhattan. He saved every dollar he could, and in 1920 he opened his own small bakery in Brooklyn.

Salvatore also made pizza. In Naples, pizza was an everyday dish for working people: cheap, fast and filling. In New York at that time, however, most Americans had never eaten pizza. Salvatore strongly believed that one day the whole country would love this simple dish. Today, pizza is an everyday food all over America.

My grandmother Rosa often told me about Sunday nights at Salvatore's house. He made the dough by hand and worked it until it was soft and smooth. "The dough must be as smooth as silk," he always said. Then he added tomatoes, cheese and a little oil. When the pizza came out of the oven, the oil made it shine. Rosa said that the whole table seemed to shine with happiness.

Salvatore was a practical man who did not waste anything. Old bread became another dish, and cold pizza became breakfast. He also strongly believed that a family should eat together. "Nobody leaves the table until the dishes are washed," he used to say.

Last month, I decided to make Salvatore's pizza for my friends. My first try was a disaster. The dough was not smooth at all, and the pizza burned in the oven. It was a complete disaster! I called Rosa, and she laughed. She said that Salvatore's first pizza in America had been a disaster too, because his new oven was too hot. She told me to try again. My second pizza was much better. My friends said it was the best pizza they had ever eaten.

Questions:
What can you find in Naples?
You can find a royal palace and one of the oldest opera houses in Europe, the San Carlo theater.
What was Salvatore's practical plan?
His plan was to find a job, save money and open his own bakery.
What did Salvatore strongly believe about pizza?
He strongly believed that one day the whole country would love it.
How did Salvatore make the dough?
He made it by hand and worked it until it was soft and smooth.
Why was the writer's first pizza a disaster?
It was a disaster because the dough was not smooth and the pizza burned in the oven.
What did Rosa say about Salvatore's first pizza in America?
She said that it had been a disaster too, because his new oven was too hot.

lessons.title: The Clockmaker from the Black Forest
lessons.summary: A family remembers a German clockmaker who came to Milwaukee in 1872.
lessons.text:
In my parents' living room, there is an old wooden clock. It was made by my great-great-great-grandfather, Johann Becker, who came from Germany to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in 1872.

Johann was born in the Black Forest, a region of hills and forests in the south of Germany. At that time, Germany was not yet one country, and his region belonged to Baden, a small state ruled by a grand duke. The Black Forest was famous for its clocks. In winter, when there was no work on the farms, many families there made clocks at home. Johann's father was a clockmaker too, and the family was proud that he had once repaired a clock for the grand duke.

Johann learned the work from his father. He understood every mechanism, from the smallest wheel to the largest spring.

In Milwaukee, many people spoke German, so Johann did not feel completely alone. He opened a small shop and worked at a wooden desk by the window. On his desk, there were always small tools, pieces of metal and the open mechanism of a clock. His output was small: he made only about 2 clocks a month, because he did everything by hand. The big factories in the East had a huge output, whereas Johann made each clock slowly. Nevertheless, people said that his clocks were the best in the city.

He also repaired alarm clocks. Many workers in Milwaukee started at the factories very early, so they needed an alarm to wake up. An alarm that did not ring was a serious problem, and people brought broken alarm clocks to his desk every day.

German has many long compound words, which are made of two or more shorter words. Kindergarten, for example, is a German compound word that means "garden for children." Johann's favorite English phrase was "Time is money." He said this phrase to his children every morning.

Johann never fully integrated into American life, but his children integrated quickly. They went to school in English and played baseball. However, they kept some elements of German life. One element was music, because the family sang German songs at Christmas. Another element was the kindergarten, which German immigrants brought to America.

In the only photo of Johann, he is an old man with gray hair and a gray beard, sitting at his desk. His clock still works. Its wooden case has turned gray with age, but every hour it rings softly, just as he planned.

Questions:
Who ruled Baden when Johann was born?
A grand duke ruled Baden.
What did Johann understand?
He understood every mechanism, from the smallest wheel to the largest spring.
Why was Johann's output small?
His output was small because he did everything by hand.
Why did workers need an alarm clock?
They needed an alarm to wake up, because they started at the factories very early.
What does the compound word "kindergarten" mean?
It means "garden for children."
What elements of German life did Johann's children keep?
They kept German music and the kindergarten.

lessons.title: Grandpa Luis, the Walker
lessons.summary: A girl interviews her grandfather, a retired mail carrier who came from Mexico in 1966.
lessons.text:
For a school project, I interviewed my grandfather, Luis Garcia. He is 78 years old, and he retired 13 years ago after more than 30 years as a mail carrier in San Antonio, Texas. He was born in Guadalajara, Mexico, and came to the United States in 1966. Here is part of our conversation.

Me: Why did you come to the United States?
Grandpa: My uncle lived in San Antonio. He wrote to us that there were good jobs here. I was 20, and I wanted to see the world.

Me: What was your first job?
Grandpa: I worked in a men's clothing store downtown. I sold suits, shirts and ties. I learned a lot of English there, because I talked to customers all day. I also learned a lot about clothing.

Me: How did you become a mail carrier?
Grandpa: A customer at the men's store was a mail carrier. He told me that the post office needed people. I became a citizen in 1972, and I started as a carrier the next year.

Me: Did you like the job?
Grandpa: I loved it. I walked about 10 miles every day. I was a fast walker, so the other carriers called me "the Walker." I knew every family and every dog on my route.

Me: Tell me about soccer.
Grandpa: Ah, soccer! In Mexico, everyone plays soccer. Here, in 1966, not many Americans watched it. So we started a team with other workers from Mexico.

Me: Were you a good player?
Grandpa: I was an offensive player, so my job was to score goals. I wasn't a star, but I was fast, and a fast offensive player is always useful. I remember one game in 1970. We were losing 3 to 0 at halftime. Then, in the second half, we had a great rally and scored 4 goals. That rally is still my favorite soccer memory.

Me: Did you ever get angry when you lost?
Grandpa: Never. My father taught me that anger never helps you win. When a player from the other team pushed me, I didn't show any anger. I just ran faster.

Me: Do you still go to Mexico?
Grandpa: Every year. Your grandmother and I take a vacation in Guadalajara every December. Now that I'm retired, our vacation lasts a whole month!

My grandfather says that being retired is wonderful, but he still walks 3 miles every morning. "Once a walker, always a walker," he says.

Questions:
What was Luis's first job in the United States?
He worked in a men's clothing store downtown.
When did he start as a mail carrier?
He started as a carrier in 1973, the year after he became a citizen.
Why did the other carriers call him "the Walker"?
They called him "the Walker" because he was a fast walker.
What was his job on the soccer team?
He was an offensive player, so his job was to score goals.
What did his father teach him?
His father taught him that anger never helps you win.
How long is his vacation in Mexico now?
Now that he is retired, his vacation lasts a whole month.

lessons.title: My Grandmother's New Life
lessons.summary: A student's essay about her grandmother, who came from Vietnam in 1975 and became a nurse.
lessons.text:
For my history class, we had to write an essay about a person in our family who came to America. I chose my grandmother, Lan Nguyen.

Lan was born in Saigon, Vietnam, in 1960. Her father was a civilian who worked in an office for an American company. In April 1975, when the war ended, many civilians who had worked with Americans left the country. Lan's family was among them. She was 15 years old.

The family first lived for several weeks at Camp Pendleton, a large military base in California. About 50,000 Vietnamese people stayed there that year. Then a church in Houston, Texas, agreed to help the family. A couple from the church, Robert and Mary Johnson, met them at the airport. That was the beginning of a long friendship. The friendship between the two families has now lasted for more than 50 years.

At first, Lan felt a lot of anxiety. Everything was new: the food, the weather and the language. Her biggest anxiety was school. Before 1975, her exposure to English had been very limited, and she knew only a few words. English spelling seemed very complicated to her. Why do some words look almost the same but sound completely different? However, daily exposure to the language helped her a lot. Mary Johnson helped her with homework every evening, and in spite of her anxiety, Lan finished high school with good grades.

Lan loved science, especially biology. She studied biology at the University of Houston and then became a nurse. She worked in healthcare for 35 years. Many of her colleagues at the hospital were immigrants too, from India, Mexico and the Philippines. One colleague, a nurse from the Philippines, became her best friend.

In 1985, Lan and my grandfather bought their first house. It was small, and they had a mortgage for 30 years. Lan told me that paying the mortgage every month had not been easy, but she had been proud of every payment. They finally paid off the mortgage in 2015.

Today, Lan is retired, but she still believes that healthcare is one of the most important jobs in the world. My mother works in healthcare too, because she is a doctor. When I asked Lan what she had learned from her life, she said that starting a new life had been complicated, but that kindness had made it easier. I agree with her, and that is why I chose her for this essay.

Questions:
Who did the student write her essay about?
She wrote her essay about her grandmother, Lan Nguyen.
What did Lan's father do?
He was a civilian who worked in an office for an American company.
Who met the family at the airport in Houston?
Robert and Mary Johnson, a couple from the church, met them at the airport.
Why did Lan feel anxiety about school?
She felt anxiety because her exposure to English had been very limited.
What did Lan study, and where did she work?
She studied biology and worked in healthcare as a nurse for 35 years.
When did Lan and her husband pay off their mortgage?
They paid off their mortgage in 2015.

lessons.title: A Day at Ellis Island
lessons.summary: A girl writes an e-mail to her aunt about visiting the Ellis Island museum and finding their family's record.
lessons.text:
Hi Aunt Carol,

We just got back to the hotel after our day at Ellis Island, and I have to tell you about it right away!

We took the boat from Battery Park in the morning. The line was ridiculous: we waited for more than an hour! Dad said we should have bought our tickets online. The boat stopped at the Statue of Liberty first, but we decided to skip the statue and stay on the boat, because we wanted lots of time on Ellis Island. We're going to visit the statue tomorrow. We didn't want to skip it completely!

The museum is in the old main building. At the door, we each got an audio guide. In the Great Hall, the audio guide played a short segment of an interview with a woman who had arrived there in 1910 as a little girl. The museum has hundreds of hours of audio in which immigrants tell their own stories. In my favorite segment, a man described his first day in New York. Each segment is only 2 or 3 minutes long, so I listened to a lot of them.

After lunch, we went to the computer room. The museum has a database of the passenger lists from the old ships. You type a name, and the database shows you the person's age, the ship and the date of arrival. Mom typed Giuseppe Conti, your grandfather's name. At first, the database found 40 men with that name, which was ridiculous! Then we added the year, 1912, and the name of his village. Shortly after that, we found him. Tommy shouted, "That's him!" so loudly that everyone in the room turned around. A woman who works there smiled and said that people shout in that room every day.

The record said that Giuseppe was 17 years old and a farmer. Mom read it aloud with tears in her eyes. Dad had tears in his eyes too, although he said it was only because of the cold air in the room. We printed a copy for you, so you can see it shortly.

The atmosphere in the whole building was quiet and kind. It felt like a place where people remember.

We are flying home on Sunday. See you shortly!

Love,
Emma

Questions:
Why did Emma's family skip the Statue of Liberty?
They skipped it because they wanted lots of time on Ellis Island.
What did the audio guide play in the Great Hall?
It played a short segment of an interview with a woman who had arrived in 1910.
What does the database show you?
It shows you the person's age, the ship and the date of arrival.
What did Tommy shout when they found Giuseppe?
He shouted, "That's him!"
Who had tears in their eyes?
Mom and Dad had tears in their eyes.

lessons.title: Citizenship Day at the Courthouse
lessons.summary: A short news report about 42 people who became American citizens on Citizenship Day.
lessons.text:
On Tuesday, September 17, which is Citizenship Day, 42 people became citizens of the United States at the federal court building in Springfield. They came from 19 countries, including Mexico, Vietnam, China, Ireland and Italy. The youngest new citizen was 18, and the oldest was 81.

The ceremony took place in a large courtroom. On the wall behind the judge's desk, there was a big seal with an eagle. The eagle, which holds an olive branch and arrows, is a symbol of the country. Judge Ellen Ortiz led the ceremony. First, the new citizens stood up and promised to be loyal to the United States. Then each of them received a certificate, and their families took photos.

In her speech, Judge Ortiz talked about the rights that all citizens share. "In this country, a person is innocent until a court decides otherwise," she said. "Even when a whole town believes that someone has done something wrong, the law treats that person as innocent. The government cannot impose a religion on you, and it cannot impose silence on you. You are free to speak, to write and to disagree."

She also reminded them that freedom comes with responsibility. "Your choices have consequences," she said. "When you vote, the consequences of your vote reach your town, your state and your country. So use your own judgment. Read, listen and ask questions, and then decide. I trust your judgment."

Judge Ortiz said that citizenship was not a gift for a small elite. "This country does not belong to an elite," she said. "It belongs to the farm worker and the doctor, to the student and the grandmother." She added that a good citizen did not necessarily have to be born here. "Being born here does not necessarily make you a better citizen. What matters is what you do for your community."

After the ceremony, many families took photos in front of the eagle. One new citizen, Maria Lopez, who came from Mexico 20 years ago, said that she had waited a long time for this day. She said that she had cried during the ceremony and that she finally felt at home. Her son, who was born in Springfield, said that he had never seen his mother so happy.

Questions:
How many people became citizens, and where did they come from?
42 people became citizens, and they came from 19 countries.
What was on the wall behind the judge's desk?
There was a big seal with an eagle.
What did Judge Ortiz say about a person in this country?
She said that a person was innocent until a court decided otherwise.
What did the judge say about voting?
She said that a vote had consequences and that people should use their own judgment.
Does a good citizen have to be born in America?
No. The judge said that a good citizen did not necessarily have to be born here.
How did Maria Lopez feel?
She said that she finally felt at home.

lessons.title: New Year in Chinatown
lessons.summary: A girl spends the Lunar New Year in San Francisco's Chinatown with her grandfather, who once danced in the lion dance.
lessons.text:
Saturday, February 10

Today was the first day of the Lunar New Year, so I spent the whole day in Chinatown with my grandfather, Wei Chen. Grandpa Wei came to San Francisco from southern China in 1968. Before 1965, the law allowed only a very small number of Chinese immigrants to come each year. A new law in 1965 changed that, and many families, like ours, could finally come.

In the morning, we went to the market to buy tangerines. Grandpa always chooses them very carefully. Each tangerine must still have its stem and a few green leaves. He says that a fruit with its stem and leaves brings good luck and a long life to the family. We also bought some flowers with long stems for the table.

The atmosphere in the streets was wonderful. Everyone was wearing red, and the shops were full of red paper decorations. People smiled and wished each other a happy new year. The atmosphere was loud, busy and happy at the same time.

In the afternoon, we watched the lion dance. The lion needs 2 dancers. One dancer is the head, and the other dancer is the tail. The head moves the eyes and the mouth, whereas the tail follows and moves the back of the lion. Grandpa said that the tail is the harder job, because you can't see anything and you have to bend down the whole time. When he was young, he danced the tail of the lion in this same street for 10 years!

After the lion dance, students from a martial arts school showed us a sword dance. Their swords were long and bright, and they moved them very fast. One girl, who was about my age, used 2 swords at the same time. I couldn't stop watching her. Then the drums started again, and the firecrackers began to snap and pop. Grandpa covered his ears and laughed.

I snapped about 100 photos with my phone, and I snapped one of Grandpa in front of the lion. In the evening, we ate dinner with the whole family, and Grandpa told the story of his lion dance days once again. Nobody minded hearing it, because he tells it so well.

Questions:
Why does Grandpa Wei choose tangerines with a stem and leaves?
He says that a fruit with its stem and leaves brings good luck and a long life to the family.
How was the atmosphere in the streets?
It was loud, busy and happy at the same time.
What do the head and the tail of the lion do?
The head moves the eyes and the mouth, whereas the tail follows and moves the back of the lion.
Why is the tail the harder job?
It is harder because you can't see anything and you have to bend down the whole time.
What did the girl in the sword dance do?
She used 2 swords at the same time.
